accuracyBoundary: These chapters teach mechanisms and decision logic. Material-grade processing windows, machine limits, mould limits, hot-runner limits and site procedures remain controlling. Numeric examples from manufacturer documents are evidence examples only and are not universal setpoints.

chapters.title: Polymer structure: amorphous and semi-crystalline behaviour
chapters.applicability: General thermoplastic injection-moulding concepts; individual grades may behave differently because of molecular architecture, additives, reinforcement and processing history.

sections.title: Structure changes processing behaviour
sections.text: Thermoplastics do not all set up in the mould in the same way. In amorphous materials, molecular movement falls away as the polymer cools through its glass-transition region. Semi-crystalline materials can also develop ordered crystalline regions as they cool. That difference shows up in shrinkage, dimensional response, cooling behaviour and the way mould temperature and cooling history influence the finished part.

sections.title: Do not turn the categories into absolutes
sections.text: Amorphous and semi-crystalline are useful starting points, not complete processing instructions. Copolymers, fillers, fibres, nucleating agents, flame-retardant packages and other modifiers can change flow, crystallisation, shrinkage and warpage significantly. When the process matters, work from the actual grade documentation and the behaviour of the real part.

chapters.title: Viscosity, shear rate, temperature and flow behaviour
chapters.applicability: Conceptual polymer-flow guidance. Quantitative viscosity behaviour requires material-specific rheological data and the relevant temperature and shear-rate range.

sections.title: Flow resistance is not a single material number
sections.text: A melt does not carry one fixed viscosity value into every moulding condition. Injection moulding usually operates in shear-dependent flow, so fill rate, melt temperature, geometry and material condition can all change the pressure needed to keep the melt moving. A viscosity number without the material identity, temperature and shear-rate basis tells only part of the story.

sections.title: Pressure is evidence about the whole flow path
sections.text: Injection pressure reflects everything the melt has to push through: the machine nozzle, runner system, gates and cavity, as well as the melt's own flow behaviour. When pressure changes, resist the temptation to name a cause from that signal alone. Compare controlled conditions, process traces and physical evidence before deciding which part of the flow path has changed.

chapters.title: Moisture, drying and hydrolysis without universal drying numbers
chapters.applicability: Hygroscopic and moisture-sensitive thermoplastics. Exact allowable moisture, dryer type, temperature and time are grade-specific and must come from current supplier guidance.

sections.title: Moisture can affect appearance, processing and polymer integrity
sections.text: Moisture problems depend on the polymer chemistry. They may appear as surface defects, foaming or unstable plasticising; in hydrolysis-sensitive materials, moisture present at melt temperature can also reduce molecular weight. That makes drying a material-control step, not simply a way to improve appearance.

sections.title: There is no universal drying recipe
sections.text: Supplier guidance shows just how different drying requirements can be from one polymer family or grade to another. Copying a time-and-temperature setting from another resin may do too little, or may damage the material. Before setting the dryer, confirm the exact grade, its incoming or measured moisture condition, the dryer capability and the current supplier requirement.

sections.title: Keep the material dry after drying
sections.text: A good drying cycle can be undone on the way to the machine. Hygroscopic material can pick moisture back up during conveying, storage or feeding if it is exposed to humid air. When moisture-related evidence continues after drying, follow the whole material path from the dryer to the feed throat rather than looking at the dryer in isolation.

chapters.title: Residence time, thermal history and degradation
chapters.applicability: General thermoplastic processing mechanism; acceptable melt temperature and residence-time exposure are grade-specific.

sections.title: Time at temperature matters
sections.text: Barrel setpoints tell only part of a polymer's thermal history. Actual melt temperature, time in the plasticising unit, delays, shot utilisation, hot-runner residence and repeated heating all add to the exposure. For engineering polymers in particular, manufacturer guidance treats residence time as part of the quality picture for good reason.

sections.title: Treat degradation as an evidence problem
sections.text: Discolouration, odour, gas, deposits, viscosity change or loss of mechanical properties can all fit a degradation mechanism, but none proves it on its own. Check the real melt conditions, residence path, interruptions, contamination risk and grade-specific limits before changing settings.

chapters.title: Commodity, engineering and high-performance polymer families
chapters.applicability: Orientation only. Family names do not replace grade-level TDS, processing guides, SDS or application qualification.

sections.title: Families are useful maps, not recipes
sections.text: A polymer family gives you a useful first picture of likely thermal behaviour, moisture sensitivity, stiffness, toughness, chemical resistance and processing demands. It helps you ask the right questions. It does not, by itself, tell you what production window to run.

sections.title: The grade is the actionable identity
sections.text: Two grades with the same family name can behave very differently because of molecular weight, reinforcement, flame retardants, impact modifiers, colour systems or processing aids. For production decisions, identify the full commercial grade and the revision of its supplier information before leaning on family-level assumptions.

chapters.title: Glass fibre, mineral, flame retardants, colour and other modifiers
chapters.applicability: General modifier effects; actual property and processing consequences are formulation- and grade-specific.

sections.title: Modifiers change the material system
sections.text: Once reinforcement or additives are introduced, you are dealing with a different material system, not just the base resin with an extra ingredient. Stiffness, flow, shrinkage, anisotropy, thermal behaviour, appearance and degradation sensitivity can all move. With fibres, orientation can also make shrinkage and properties directional, linking gate position, flow pattern and part geometry directly to warpage and dimensional behaviour.

sections.title: Do not transfer settings between modified grades by name alone
sections.text: Treat a reinforced, flame-retarded or otherwise modified grade as its own processing material. Check the supplier's grade-specific processing guidance and qualification requirements instead of assuming that settings from an unfilled or differently modified grade will carry across.

chapters.title: Screw, barrel, non-return valve and plasticising
chapters.applicability: Reciprocating-screw injection units. Screw geometry, non-return-valve design, allowable temperatures and wear limits are machine/material specific.

sections.title: Plasticising prepares the next shot
sections.text: During screw recovery, pellets move forward, heat, compress and mix while the screw travels rearward to build the next shot. The barrel heaters supply part of the energy, but screw work and the material's own response also shape the final melt condition.

sections.title: The non-return valve matters during injection
sections.text: During injection, the check ring or other non-return system is there to limit reverse flow so forward screw movement displaces melt toward the mould. Wear, contamination or poor sealing can contribute to shot-to-shot variation, but cushion or part-weight movement is not automatic proof of a valve fault. Look for repeatable evidence before blaming the hardware.

sections.title: Hardware suitability is material dependent
sections.text: Material suppliers may specify suitable screw designs, lengths, compression characteristics and nozzle arrangements for their grades. Those requirements take precedence over any generic description in this Book.

chapters.title: Shot size, cushion, screw position and machine suitability
chapters.applicability: General reciprocating-screw process reasoning. Machine manufacturer limits and material residence constraints control acceptable utilisation.

sections.title: Screw position is process evidence
sections.text: The screw-position trace tells the story of how the injection unit moved through dosing, filling, transfer and packing. Cushion is the remaining forward-stroke position after the programmed injection and hold sequence, but the number only makes sense in the context of that machine's position convention and control architecture.

sections.title: Avoid universal shot-utilisation percentages
sections.text: A machine can be a poor fit for a job for several different reasons: excessive residence exposure, limited plasticising capacity, insufficient injection pressure or rate, poor metering repeatability, clamp requirements, or simply the wrong working range. No single utilisation percentage can settle that question. Judge the machine, material, mould and required process window as one system.

chapters.title: Injection velocity, pressure and machine control
chapters.applicability: General filling-control concepts. Controller terminology, limits and transfer behaviour are machine-specific.

sections.title: Velocity command and pressure demand are different quantities
sections.text: In velocity-controlled filling, the machine tries to move the screw to the commanded velocity profile while pressure rises as needed to overcome resistance, up to the machine or programmed limit. If the process runs out of available pressure, the commanded velocity may never be reached.

sections.title: A process should distinguish control from limits
sections.text: A pressure limit that is constantly clipping the fill is not the same thing as a deliberately pressure-controlled filling strategy. Look at the actual velocity, pressure and position traces to see what the machine achieved, not just what the setup screen asked for.

sections.title: Transfer changes the control objective
sections.text: At transfer, the job of the control system changes from filling the cavity toward managing post-fill pressure. The transfer position or other criterion therefore has to be read alongside the mould filling state, machine response and process evidence. A transfer number that works on one mould is not a portable recipe for another.
